replacement: “Be convinced, then, that this adventure abroad will increase our power at home. Let us make the expedition and humble the pride of the Peloponnesians. Let us sail off to Sicily and show them how little we care for the peace we are now enjoying. At the same time we shall either become masters of the whole of Hellas, as we very easily may, through the accession of the Sicilian Hellenes, or at any rate ruin the Syracusans, to the no small advantage of ourselves and our allies. Our navy will secure our freedom to stay if we succeed or to return, for we shall be superior at sea to all the Siceliots put together. Do not let Nicias turn you from your purpose, with the do-nothing policy he advocates and his setting of the young against the old. Follow the good old fashion by which our fathers, old and young together, brought our affairs to their present height by their united counsels, and endeavor still to advance them. Understand that neither youth nor old age can do anything without the other, and that levity, sobriety and deliberate judgment are strongest when united. Understand too that if the city sinks into inaction, it will wear itself out like everything else, and its skill in everything will decay, while each fresh struggle will give it fresh experience and make it more used to defending itself not in word but in deed. In short, my conviction is that a city not inactive by nature could choose no quicker way to ruin itself than by suddenly adopting such a policy. The safest rule of life is to take one’s character and institutions for better and for worse, and to live up to them as closely as one can.”

"Nearly" added before "the whole population", altering the source's "one may say" hedge.
replacement: After this the departure for Sicily took place, at about midsummer. Most of the allies, with the corn transports, the smaller craft and the rest of the expedition, had already been ordered to gather at Corcyra, so as to cross the Ionian Sea from there together to the Iapygian promontory. The Athenians themselves, with those of their allies who happened to be present, went down to Piraeus on the appointed day at daybreak and began to man the ships to put out to sea. The whole population of the city, one may say, went down with them, citizens and foreigners alike. The people of the country each escorted their own, whether friends, relatives or sons, with hope and with lamentation as they went. They thought of the conquests they hoped to make, or of the friends they might never see again, given the long voyage ahead of them, away from their country. At this moment, as they were about to part, the danger came home to them more than when they voted for the expedition. Even so, the strength of the armament and the lavish provision they saw in every department could not but comfort them. The foreigners and the rest of the crowd simply came to see a sight worth seeing and beyond belief.
